newsitem.title: INDIA: India Ashok Leyland net seen up 18 pct.
newsitem.headline: India Ashok Leyland net seen up 18 pct.

text.p: Robust sales in commercial vehicles are expected to push up truck maker Ashok Leyland Ltd's net profit by about 18 percent in 1996/97 (April-March) compared with 1995/96, analysts said.

Ashok Leyland is the second largest commercial vehicle manufacturer in India and is due to announce its results on Wednesday, July 2. The company's shares are currently trading at a 12-month low of 67.75 rupees.
"Ashok Leyland has had good sales this year, with production of trucks climbing by close to 20 percent," auto analyst K.N. Srinivasan at Jardine Fleming said.
He added that the company's main product line of medium commercial vehicles had done well, and continued to be the driving force behind the company.

"One of the factors that is expected to keep net profit growth from being higher than 18 percent is the company's tax burden. With depreciation falling sharply, tax could be 25 percent higher than last year," Srinivasan said.
Analysts said they expected Ashok Leyland's net profit to be in the region of 1.35 billion rupees ($37.7 million) in 1996/97 (April-March) from 1.1 billion rupees in 1995/96.
Sales were expected to touch an average 25 billion rupees in 1996/97, analysts said. Ashok Leyland's sales for 1996/97 were 20.6 billion rupees.

"A seven percent growth in the economy and the freight constraints of the railways helped Ashok Leyland to increase its sales," said an analyst with a leading French investment house who did not want to be identified.

Analysts expect the company's net profit in 1997/98 to touch 1.5 billion rupees, a growth of less than 15 percent. Sales would climb faster at an average 20 percent to reach the 30 billion rupee mark, they said.
They said slower net profit growth in 1997/98 could be attributed to the low sales of its Cargo line of trucks, and enhanced competition from India's largest truck maker, Telco.

Rohit Rana, auto analyst at Socgen Crosby said: "Competition from Telco will be severe this year, as it plans to launch trucks in the seven-tonne, 14-tonne, 35-tonne and 40-tonne gross vehicle weight range. These are Ashok Leyland's bread and butter lines."

He added that the company was constrained by Telco's pricing policy. "It can only raise prices if Telco does. Telco chose not to do so last year, and this has forced Ashok Leyland to keep its prices down."
Analysts are still waiting for the company's latest product, the Cargo line, produced in collaboration with Italian carmaker Fiat's Iveco truck unit, to live up to expectations.
"The volumes of the Cargo line have not picked up. Of the 43,500 trucks that the company sold in 1996/97, less than 5,000 were Cargos," said Jardine's Srinivasan.
He said Cargo was Ashok Leyland's product of the future, but its acceptance levels were still low due to high prices. "The company's tried and tested Leyland range continues to be its mainstay."
